newsitem.title: POLAND: New Polish constitution aims to entrench democracy.
newsitem.headline: New Polish constitution aims to entrench democracy.

text.p: Poland's new constitution, which exit polls suggest was adopted in a referendum on Sunday, is meant to crown the triumph of democracy over communism eight years ago but it has aroused fierce controversy.
"Out of care for the existence and future of our homeland, which in 1989 regained the sovereign and democratic ability to determine its own destiny..." begins the preamble.
In an bid to include those who stress the role of religion in defining the largely Catholic country's identity as well as people of other faiths or none, it aims to be all-inclusive.

"We, the Polish Nation, all citizens of the Republic, equally those believing in God as the source of truth, justice, goodness and beauty and those not sharing that faith and drawing these universal values from other sources..." it says before enjoining respect for human dignity, freedom and solidarity.
Much of the right-wing opposition, which had proposed its own alternative constitution, says this wording underlines divisions in society rather than a common sense of nationhood.
A major objection raised by some rightist parties stressing patriotic values is article 90, which provides for future entry into international structures such as the European Union.

"The Polish Republic can on the basis of international treaty cede to an international organisation or international organ prerogatives of organs of state authority in certain matters," the disputed article says.

Although the constitution says such a decision must be taken by a two-thirds parliamentary majority and may be confirmed by referendum, some critics say this article could one day be abused to undermine Poland's hard-won sovereignty.
The constitution broadly upholds the current political system but weakens the presidency in favour of parliament, a move condemned by former president Lech Walesa.

For example, the president will no longer be able to use his veto to block the national budget and a smaller parliamentary majority, three-fifths rather than two-thirds, will suffice to overrule his veto on other issues.
The fundamental law bans fascist, communist and racist political parties advocating totalitarianism.
On the economy, it safeguards public finances but contains welfare state provisions which some say Poland can ill afford. @

These include obliging the government to act to curb unemployment and stimulate housing construction while guaranteeing free publicly funded basic health care, free basic education for all and a minimum wage.
Most economists praise the charter for capping public debt at 60 percent of gross domestic product and forbidding the government to finance the budget deficit in the central bank.
The constitution guarantees civil and economic liberties.
It keeps the state and the Catholic Church separate, a concept which pro-Catholic rightist parties have found unnerving in view of past Communist persecution of the Church.

The Church and its backers on the political right, notably the Solidarity trade union, had wanted a clause protecting human life from conception to natural death which would have effectively banned abortion -- legalised in Poland last year.
Instead, the issue remains open. "The Polish Republic assures every person the right to legal protection of life."
The constitution's authors argue that they have tried to consider and incorporate all suggestions where possible, while producing a modern, European-style democratic constitution.
But even they often admit it is over-long and the wording of the document, drafted by parliamentary committee amid years of tough negotiations, lacks grace.

Prominent Polish poet and right-wing commentator Zbigniew Herbert, who opposed the constitution on grounds of principle, was damning on its style. "It is over-detailed and written in appalling Polish," Herbert told Wprost weekly. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
